topic: Sumer, and the Anunnaki conspiracy theory
title: Sumer and the Anunnaki: The Real Civilization and the Modern Conspiracy Theory
department: Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations, Assyriology Program
description: An introduction to Sumer, the civilization of southern Mesopotamia that built some of the world's first cities and developed cuneiform, one of the first writing systems, followed by an honest look at the conspiracy theory built on it. The first five chapters teach the real Sumer from its tablets and ruins: cities, writing, kings and the Sumerian King List, gods and myths, and Gilgamesh. The last three examine Zecharia Sitchin's claim, from The 12th Planet (1976), that the Anunnaki were astronauts from a hidden planet called Nibiru, setting what he said the tablets say beside what Assyriologists read in them, and checking the Nibiru doomsday predictions against astronomy. The evidence does not support the theory, and the book shows exactly why while taking the reader's curiosity seriously.
objectives: Locate the main Sumerian cities on a map and describe how a Sumerian city worked: temple, palace, irrigation, crafts and trade.
Explain how cuneiform grew from bookkeeping into a script for literature, and how scholars read a tablet today.
Describe the main periods of Sumerian history and the evidence (excavation, inscriptions, king lists) used to date them.
Summarize the main Sumerian gods and myths, including the Anunnaki as the texts describe them, using scholarly translations.
Retell the story of Gilgamesh and explain how the Sumerian poems relate to the later Babylonian epic.
State Zecharia Sitchin's main claims fairly and compare each with what Assyriologists read in the same texts.
Explain why astronomy rules out a hidden planet Nibiru and why each predicted Nibiru doomsday passed without event.
Apply the claim-checking method shared with ARC 101 to a new claim about the ancient Near East.

sections.title: Giving Sumer back to the Sumerians
sections.summary: What the real civilization achieved, and a final checklist for claims about the ancient world, shared with ARC 101.

preface:
You asked about a Sumerian conspiracy, and this book will take you there. First, though, it takes you to Sumer itself, because the real civilization is the part most people never hear about, and it is extraordinary. In the cities of what is now southern Iraq, more than four thousand years ago, people raised temples on great stepped platforms, kept accounts in wedge-shaped writing on clay, wrote down laws, and told stories about Gilgamesh, a king who went looking for a way not to die.

The first five chapters teach Sumer from its own evidence: excavated cities, tablets, the Sumerian King List, the gods and the myths, read in the translations scholars use. The last three turn to the modern idea, made famous by Zecharia Sitchin's The 12th Planet in 1976, that the gods called the Anunnaki were astronauts from a hidden planet named Nibiru. We will state his claims fairly, set each one beside what specialists read in the same tablets, and then look at the sky to see whether a planet could be hiding there.

I will not keep you in suspense. The tablets do not say what Sitchin said they say, astronomers have found no Nibiru, and every predicted Nibiru doomsday has come and gone. Knowing exactly why is a skill worth having. It uses the same toolkit as our book on ancient-astronaut claims (ARC 101), and by the end you will be able to check a claim about the ancient world against the evidence yourself.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an Assyriologist would: from excavated sites and tablets, read through standard editions and translations (the ETCSL, George's Gilgamesh), and, in Chapters 6 to 8, from Sitchin's own books set beside what scholars read in the same texts and what astronomers observe.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know the real Sumer from its own words, and you will be able to check any claim about the Anunnaki or Nibiru against the tablets and the sky.
threads: Read the texts themselves: every statement about what Sumerians believed is checked against a scholarly translation.

How we know: The archaeologist's toolkit, shared by ARC 101, EGY 101 and ANE 101: context (where a thing was found and with what), stratigraphy (lower layers are older), dating methods that check each other (radiocarbon, tree rings, inscriptions and king lists, styles of pottery and objects), materials analysis, written texts read in the original, and experimental archaeology.
The real Sumer is remarkable on its own: cities, writing, law, literature and mathematics.
Fair comparison: each modern claim is stated as its author wrote it, then set beside the evidence.

conventions: Sumerian and Akkadian words in italics with a translation; divine names in standard modern spellings (An, Enlil, Enki, Inanna, Anunnaki).
Cite Sumerian literary compositions by their ETCSL title and catalogue number.
Dates as BC with 'about'; note once that Mesopotamian dates follow the conventional Middle Chronology, and give the evidence behind key dates.
Quote Sitchin's claims from his own books, and scholars' readings from published translations; never put words in either's mouth.
Cross-reference ARC 101 (the ancient-astronaut idea and claim-checking) and EGY 101 (shared dating and materials methods) by chapter.

bible.care: The reader asked about a 'Sumerian conspiracy'. The book teaches the real Sumer first, from its texts and archaeology, then presents Zecharia Sitchin's Anunnaki and Nibiru claims accurately as modern claims that Assyriologists and astronomers reject, showing the evidence point by point. Never present the claims as fact or as a live scholarly debate, and never mock the reader or people who find the claims persuasive; criticize arguments, not people. Present Sumerian religion respectfully and in its own terms and sources, as the beliefs of an ancient people, keeping it distinct both from historical reconstruction and from modern claims about it. Doomsday predictions frighten some people: state plainly that each predicted date passed without event and that no hidden planet threatens Earth. Sitchin's books are quoted as the source of the claims, never cited as evidence.
